title: Alignment Layer for Embeddings & Rerank: Paging Semantics, HTTP Status Mapping, and Degradation Strategy
creator: Jordan Kim
description:
Problem: Multiple client SDKs and legacy endpoints interpret embeddings and rerank pagination, error codes, and streaming semantics differently. This causes intermittent client-side infinite loops (cursor misread), inconsistent retry behavior across SDKs, and poor developer experience during rollouts.

Goal: Produce a lightweight alignment layer (adapter) that normalizes paging tokens, maps internal runtime errors to a stable HTTP status taxonomy, and defines graceful degradation rules that preserve streaming/function-calling and structured output behaviors for older clients. The adapter should be opt-in via a routing flag and behind a migration window for existing customers.
acceptance_criteria: Adapter normalizes cursor formats: legacy base64 tombstone cursors and modern tokenized iterators mapped to canonical cursor V2
HTTP error mapping documented: internal transient vs throttling vs validation vs out-of-capacity mapped to 429/503/400/500 as appropriate
Client-visible pagination headers (Link, X-Next-Cursor) follow a single documented contract and are present for both streaming and non-streaming responses
Backcompat shim toggled by routing config; no change in hosted API behavior unless routing flag enabled
Integration tests exercising retry semantics, idempotency, and tombstone handling for both embeddings and rerank endpoints pass in CI
Migration playbook published with sample client changes and recommended rollout path
notes: 2025-02-17: Kickoff with Engineering and DX. Agreed adapter should be stateless and sidecar-friendly so it can sit in front of both embeddings and rerank services.
2025-02-21: Design decision: use canonical cursor V2 (JSON-safe, RFC3986-encoded) instead of forced opaque base64 to make debugging easier for customers.

2025-02-25: Trade-off: full streaming + page-link preservation requires dual-mode responses. We'll implement a hybrid where streaming responses include chunked Link heuristics and a final X-Next-Cursor header on stream termination.
2025-02-28: Security/Privacy note: adapter must not leak internal lease or node IDs. Strip internal trace metadata from cursor payloads.
2025-03-03: PM review with Solutions Eng: include a deprecation header for legacy cursor variants to encourage client upgrade within migration window.

implementation_plan: 1) Engineering spike to validate sidecar latency and resource overhead (ENG)
2) Build adapter core: cursor canonicalizer, status mapper, header normalizer (ENG)
3) Add streaming-aware Link heuristics and final-stream cursor emission (ENG)
4) Add routing flag and per-customer toggles in control plane (Platform)
5) Publish SDK migration snippets for python/node/go (DX)
6) Run canary on 10% traffic and validate telemetry (Observability)
7) Ramp per migration playbook and monitor error/regression dashboards
rollback_plan: If we observe >1% client-facing error increase or unhandled cursor regressions within 48h of canary, flip routing flag off and automatically redirect affected customers to legacy route. Post-rollback: capture full request traces, perform postmortem, and open follow-up bug tickets.
test_plan: Unit tests for cursor translation matrix covering legacy opaque tokens, tombstones, and V2 encoding
Integration tests: end-to-end embeddings -> rerank with simulated partial failures to ensure idempotent retries
Load test: sidecar under 10k rps with mixed streaming/non-streaming patterns
SDK tests: python/node/go samples validate parsing of X-Next-Cursor and Link header
migration_playbook: Provide staged instructions: (A) opt-in customers enable adapter flag; (B) observe for 7 days; (C) request SDK upgrade; (D) flip default route for new accounts after 30 days; include rollback steps and communication templates for support teams.
open_questions: Do we include an explicit TTL inside canonical cursor V2 for tombstone eviction, or let backend decide?
How should streaming partial responses indicate a transient cursor when the stream is interrupted mid-way? Explicit header or terminal event?
Do we need a specific telemetry metric for "cursor-translation-failure" vs general 4xx/5xx to simplify runbooks?
